title: Noble gases and stable outer shells
keyIdea: The noble gases in Group 0 (helium, neon, argon and the rest) hardly react, because their outer shell of electrons is already full: 2 for helium, 8 for the others. Other atoms react in ways that give them the same full outer shell. Metals lose electrons, non-metals gain them, and some atoms share them.

kid: Helium, neon and argon are the noble gases. They sit in the last column of the periodic table, Group 0. They almost never react with anything.
The reason is their electrons. Helium has 2, and its only shell holds 2. Neon is 2,8 and argon is 2,8,8. Their outer shells are full, with no gaps.
That makes them safe to use. Balloons are filled with helium, not hydrogen. Hydrogen is lighter, but it burns. Helium will not burn at all.

Other atoms are not full. Sodium is 2,8,1. It can drop its 1 outer electron and look like neon. Chlorine is 2,8,7. It can take 1 more and look like argon. Atoms take the shortest route to a full shell.
adult: Group 0 holds the noble gases: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon. They exist as single atoms and are very unreactive. Helium's outer shell holds 2 electrons and is full; the others have 8 in their outer shell.

A full outer shell is a stable arrangement, so these atoms have nothing to gain by losing, gaining or sharing electrons. Their uses depend on this. Helium fills balloons because it is light and does not burn. Argon fills filament lamps because the hot metal filament would burn in oxygen but does not react with argon.

Other atoms react in ways that give them a noble-gas arrangement. Metals with 1 to 3 outer electrons lose them: sodium 2,8,1 becomes Na⁺, 2,8, like neon. Non-metals with 5 to 7 gain electrons: chlorine 2,8,7 becomes Cl⁻, 2,8,8, like argon. Atoms halfway, such as carbon 2,4, share pairs of electrons instead, as in methane, CH₄.

Common mistakes: thinking sodium is stable because its inner shell is full, when only the outer shell counts. Saying helium is lighter than hydrogen. Thinking chlorine loses 7 electrons instead of gaining 1. Be careful too: the full-shell rule is a model. Xenon forms a few compounds with fluorine, so 'noble' means very unreactive, not never.

familyTip: Draw an egg box with 8 holes and use dried beans as electrons. Fill it to match an atom, such as 7 beans for chlorine. Ask: is it quicker to add beans or take them away to get a full box? Then try 1 bean for sodium.

worked.title: Why is a balloon filled with helium and not hydrogen, even though hydrogen is lighter?
steps: Hydrogen has 1 electron. Its only shell holds 2, so it is not full.
So hydrogen reacts: mixed with air and lit, it burns, sometimes with a bang.
Helium has 2 electrons, which fills its only shell. A full outer shell is stable, so helium does not burn or react.
Helium is a little heavier than hydrogen but still far lighter than air, so it floats safely.

practice.prompt: Why are the noble gases so unreactive?
choices: Their outer shell of electrons is full
They are heavier than other gases
practice.hint: Look at the outer shell of helium, neon and argon.
practice.explain: Helium is 2, neon 2,8 and argon 2,8,8. With a full outer shell, they have no need to lose, gain or share electrons.

practice.prompt: A metal atom has {n} electrons in its outer shell, which is shell {s}. How many electrons does it lose to get a full outer shell?
practice.hint: Give away every electron in shell {s}. Shell {=s-1} underneath is already full.
practice.explain: It loses all {n} electrons in shell {s}. Shell {=s-1}, which is full, becomes the outer shell: a noble-gas arrangement.

practice.prompt: A non-metal atom has {n} electrons in its outer shell, which is shell {s} and can hold 8. How many electrons does it gain to fill it?
practice.hint: Count the empty places left in shell {s}.
practice.explain: 8 − {n} = {=8-n}, so it gains {=8-n} electrons. Shell {s} is then full, like the noble gas at the end of row {s}.

practice.prompt: Why are filament lamps filled with argon instead of air?
choices: Argon does not react with the hot filament
practice.hint: What would oxygen in air do to a white-hot metal wire?
practice.explain: Oxygen would react with the hot filament and burn through it. Argon, 2,8,8, has a full outer shell and does not react.

practice.prompt: Which noble gas has only 2 electrons in its outer shell?
practice.hint: Which noble gas has only one shell?
practice.explain: Helium's only shell holds 2, so 2 is full. Neon and argon have 8 in their outer shells.

pool.prompt: Which electron arrangement has a full outer shell?
pool.hint: Only the last number counts. Is that shell full?
pool.explain: 2,8,8 is argon: the outer shell holds 8. 2,8,1 and 2,8,6 have gaps in their outer shells.

pool.prompt: Sodium is 2,8,1. Its second shell is full. Why is sodium still very reactive?
choices: Its outer shell has only 1 electron
Its second shell is too full
pool.hint: Which shell takes part in reactions?
pool.explain: Only the outer shell matters. Sodium's outer shell has 1 of 8, so it reacts by losing that electron.

pool.prompt: A metal atom has {n} electrons in shell {s}, its outer shell. It loses them to form an ion. What is the size of the positive charge on the ion?
pool.hint: Each electron lost leaves one more proton than electrons.
pool.explain: Losing {n} electrons leaves {n} more protons than electrons, so the ion has a {n}+ charge. Its outer shell is now shell {=s-1}, which is full.

pool.prompt: A non-metal atom has {n} electrons in shell {s}, its outer shell. It gains electrons to form an ion. What is the size of the negative charge on the ion?
pool.hint: How many empty places are there in a shell that holds 8? Each electron gained adds one negative charge.
pool.explain: It gains 8 − {n} = {=8-n} electrons, so the ion has a {=8-n}− charge and a full shell {s}.

pool.prompt: Carbon is 2,4. How does it usually get a full outer shell?
choices: It shares electrons with other atoms
pool.hint: Losing or gaining 4 electrons would both be hard.
pool.explain: Carbon shares pairs of electrons, as in methane, CH₄. Then it counts 8 in its outer shell.

pool.prompt: Chlorine is 2,8,7. What does it do to reach a full outer shell?
pool.explain: Gaining 1 electron gives 2,8,8, like argon. Losing 7 would take far more, and losing 1 leaves 2,8,6.

pool.prompt: Hydrogen is lighter than helium. Why are party balloons filled with helium?
choices: Helium does not burn because its outer shell is full
Hydrogen has a full outer shell
pool.hint: Think about what happens if a hydrogen balloon meets a flame.
pool.explain: Hydrogen's shell is half full, so it burns. Helium's only shell is full, so it is safe.

pool.prompt: After a sodium atom loses one electron, which noble gas has the same arrangement?
pool.explain: 2,8,1 minus 1 is 2,8, which is neon's arrangement.

visual.caption: Full outer shell or not? Look at the last number in each arrangement. Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: test helium and argon against hydrogen and air, mark the full outer shells, then move electrons to reach a noble-gas arrangement.
